strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: posterior sampling for masked discrete diffusion models with purely discrete token embeddings, where prior methods (G2D2, SGDD, SVDD-PM) struggle due to non-differentiability or exponential complexity. The paper is, to my knowledge, the first scalable inverse-problem solver on this class of priors.

The variational analysis (Theorems A.1/A.2) is carried out cleanly, correctly recovering the standard masked-diffusion NELBO when measurements are absent, and explicitly identifying the per-step likelihood-tilt and adaptation-gap terms; the case-by-case KL computations are correct.

Comprehensive and mostly well-designed experiments: multiple linear and nonlinear tasks on FFHQ and ImageNet, ablations (Fig. 6) that disentangle quantized expectation from anchored remasking, a control experiment against G2D2 under an identical prior and compute budget (Table 5), a larger 1000-sample evaluation (Table 7), and runtime/memory/step comparisons (Table 6).

Practically efficient: only 15 reverse steps with gradients computed w.r.t. lightweight logits rather than the 8B denoiser, with strong empirical gains (e.g., 22.7% LPIPS over PSLD at 1024x1024 Gaussian deblur at lower runtime).

Reproducibility is well supported: public codebase, detailed Algorithm 1, hyperparameter sweeps, exact evaluation protocols and image lists; limitations (tokenizer quality, weaker base model, style-extractor dependence) and an ethics statement with failure cases are honestly presented.
weaknesses: The link between the theory and the practical algorithm is loose. Theorem 3.2 bounds -log p_phi(x|y) under expectations over the true forward path q(Z|x), but the algorithm replaces ground-truth x with the model's own prediction (Eq. 7) and optimizes a per-step surrogate; the tilt q(y|x_phi(Zt)) is not a true likelihood of y given zt. The bound therefore motivates, but does not justify, the actual procedure, and no result characterizes the stationary/target distribution actually sampled.

In practice the method is test-time optimization (100 Adam steps on logits per reverse step, tuned learning rate, VGG perceptual loss) rather than principled 'posterior sampling'. The paper never evaluates posterior fidelity—no diversity, coverage, or posterior-consistency metrics are reported; only point-estimate metrics (LPIPS/PSNR/SSIM). Whether APS samples the posterior or produces a single MAP-like reconstruction is left open.

Some headline gains conflate algorithmic contributions with prior strength. The main tables compare against G2D2/SGDD using older priors while APS uses an 8B MMaDA prior plus perceptual loss; the upsampled 512/1024 protocol (APS-L) further advantages it over baselines evaluated at 256. The cleanest evidence for the algorithm itself is Table 5, which shows solid but smaller gains (~4% LPIPS).

Quantized expectation and anchored remasking are heuristics: quantizing the expected embedding via sign and straight-through estimation is only loosely related to the derived objective, and the anchor threshold schedule is borrowed from MMaDA without analysis of how sensitive results are to it. There is also no theoretical guarantee that optimizing logits toward the measurement preserves the prior distribution.

Stylization results are overstated. In Table 3, APS (ImageReward 0.63, DINO 0.41) is clearly below RB-Modulation (1.18, 0.73) and IP-Adapter on DINO; the text selectively claims superiority over weaker continuous baselines. Text-guided block inpainting additionally requires fine-tuning MMaDA with L_DDPS on 100K fashion images, which sits awkwardly with the 'training-free' framing.

Presentation issues: SVDD-PM appears as a baseline in Table 1 without introduction in the main baselines section; heavy notation in Section 3 makes the pipeline hard to follow; the distinction between Theorems 3.1/3.2 and their appendix restatements is redundant; and the perceived-quality claims in figures rest on cherry-picked qualitative examples.

strengths: Targets a genuinely underexplored problem: training-free posterior sampling with masked discrete diffusion models with purely discrete token embeddings, where existing discrete samplers (G2D2, SGDD) demonstrably struggle or fail to scale.

The variational derivations (Theorems 3.1/A.1 and 3.2/A.2) are cleanly presented and correctly reduce to the standard masked-diffusion NELBO when measurements are absent; the decomposition into reconstruction, per-step KL, adaptation gap, and likelihood-tilt terms is pedagogically useful.

Broad experimental coverage: linear and nonlinear inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet, comparison against both discrete and continuous baselines, stylization and block-inpainting applications, an ablation (Figure 6, §B.3) that disentangles quantized expectation from anchored remasking, a controlled prior-matched comparison against G2D2 (Table 5), and an efficiency analysis (Table 6).

The paper is transparent about practical choices (hyperparameter sweep in Table 4), includes failure cases (Figure 14), an honest limitations section, and a thoughtful ethics statement about posterior-sampling ambiguity in forensic contexts.
Computational efficiency is a real advantage: ~15 reverse steps and ~55–121 s per image, substantially cheaper than continuous latent-diffusion posterior samplers at comparable quality.
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and algorithm. Theorems 3.1/3.2 bound a variational family with likelihood-tilted transitions, but Algorithm 1 is essentially per-step test-time optimization of logits (100 Adam steps × 15 reverse steps) with an L1 reconstruction loss, a VGG perceptual loss, and an optional prior-preservation loss. Neither the perceptual loss, the L1 loss (inconsistent with the Gaussian likelihood assumed in the theory), nor the anchored remasking heuristic is covered by the bounds; the theory reads as motivation rather than an analysis of the method actually evaluated.

Theoretical novelty is limited: the results follow from a straightforward Jensen's-inequality argument on a tilted reverse kernel, and the anchored remasking idea is a training-free adaptation of ADLM (Rout et al., 2025a) while quantized expectation is a straight-through-estimator trick standard in VQ-VAE literature.

Evaluation fairness concerns. APS/APS-L upsample benchmark images to 512/1024, solve the problem at high resolution, and downsample to 256 for evaluation (following the G2D2 protocol), while most baselines operate at 256. APS-L's headline gains (e.g., 35.82% LPIPS on ImageNet SR) partly reflect the extra capacity/resolution of the prior rather than the sampler; the prior-matched comparison (Table 5) shows much smaller gains (PSNR 25.46→26.80). Additionally, runtimes in Table 6 mix hardware (A6000 vs A100), complicating the efficiency claims.

Main quantitative results are based on only 100 images per setting; the 1000-sample evaluation appears only for a single task (FFHQ SR, Table 7). Variance/significance of the reported improvements is not discussed, and several entries (SGDD, DAPS on general problems) are missing due to baseline limitations without substitution.

The stylization comparison overstates the contribution: Table 3 shows APS loses substantially on DINO (0.41 vs 0.89 for IP-Adapter) and trails RB-Modulation on ImageReward; the text selectively emphasizes wins on ImageReward/CLIP-T. Qualitative figure claims (e.g., buttoned shirt in Figure 5) rest on a small number of cherry-picked examples.

The 'training-free' framing is undermined by §B.8.2, where MMaDA is fine-tuned on 100K fashion images using the LDDPS objective for the block-inpainting application; this caveat is buried in the appendix.

Several algorithmic details are underspecified for reproducibility: the adaptive anchor threshold τt is described only as 'based on the cosine schedule from MMaDA,' and the interaction between the inner optimization loop, CFG scale, and the remasking schedule is not analyzed; no explicit code release is promised.
The motivating claim that SGDD 'suffers from exponential complexity' is supported only by a citation to a book draft (Chewi, 2023) rather than a derivation or measurement in this paper's setting.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: the paper identifies a genuine gap—no posterior sampler exists for masked discrete diffusion models with purely discrete token embeddings—and positions itself carefully against G2D2 (continuous relaxations), SGDD (exponential rejection rates), and derivative-free guidance (weak signals).

The two algorithmic contributions are sensible and well-differentiated: quantized expectation restores differentiability by pushing gradients through an expected codebook embedding with a straight-through estimator (avoiding the sparse updates of policy-gradient approaches), and anchored remasking uses the joint posterior estimate rather than per-token prior confidence to choose which tokens to decode early.

Extensive experiments across linear (SR, Gaussian deblur, inpainting, motion deblur) and nonlinear (HDR, nonlinear blur) inverse problems on both FFHQ and ImageNet, with quantitative tables, many qualitative figures, and a dedicated ablation (Figure 6, APS-I vs APS-II) that disentangles the contribution of each component.

A controlled comparison under an identical prior and compute budget (Table 5, APS vs G2D2 on VQ-Diffusion with 100 steps / 30 inner optimization steps) strengthens the claim that gains come from the algorithm rather than a stronger backbone.
Thorough efficiency analysis (Table 6) demonstrating substantial runtime advantages over continuous latent-space samplers, and scalability to 1024x1024 (APS-L).

Good supporting material: pseudocode (Algorithm 1), hyperparameter sweeps (Table 4), failure cases (Figure 14), an honest limitations section (tokenizer quality, weaker base model than Flux/SD3.5, stylization dependence on the style extractor), and ethics/reproducibility statements.

The theory (Theorems 3.1/3.2) is a clean variational decomposition that correctly recovers the standard masked-diffusion NELBO when measurements are absent, and the proofs in Appendix A appear correct.
weaknesses: There is a notable gap between the theoretical bounds and the practical algorithm. Theorems 3.1/3.2 derive variational upper bounds, but the implementation (per-step Adam optimization on logits, L1 measurement loss, VGG perceptual loss, prior preservation term with lambda_pp=0, STE) departs substantially from directly minimizing the bound; the theoretical contribution is thus more of a justification/motivation than a derivation of the method. The connection between Equation (7) and Algorithm 1 deserves tighter justification.

Some baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: the headline results use the MMaDA prior (512/1024 resolution with upsampling protocol) against continuous samplers using SD-based priors at 256, so part of the improvement may come from the different prior and evaluation resolution rather than the sampler itself. Table 5 partially addresses this but only for one task and 100 images.

Quantitative evaluation is limited to 100 images per benchmark (with a 1000-image check only for FFHQ SR); confidence intervals or variance estimates are not reported, making some of the smaller claimed improvements (e.g., LPIPS gains of a few percent) hard to assess.

The stylization results are comparatively weak on objective metrics (Table 3: DINO 0.41 vs 0.89 for IP-Adapter, ImageReward 0.63 vs 1.18 for RB-Modulation); the paper's claim of 'surpassing' continuous baselines holds only on a subset of metrics, and the text-guided block inpainting experiment requires fine-tuning MMaDA on 100K images, which conflicts with the 'training-free' framing.

The inner optimization loop (100 Adam steps at each of 15 reverse steps) means the method is substantially more expensive per reverse step than plain sampling; the 15-step vs 1000-step comparison in Table 6 does not fully reflect total FLOPs, and sensitivity to the number of inner steps is not ablated.

Presentation issues: the abstract/introduction overstates the theory's role ('theoretical results' as a first-class contribution), the described 'small decaying learning rate' of 1.0 is not small, and the continuous baseline DAPS actually outperforms APS on FFHQ SR/Gaussian deblur in Table 1, which the prose does not explicitly acknowledge.

strengths: Well-grounded theory: Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 derive variational upper bounds on the discrete diffusion posterior log-likelihood, connecting likelihood tilting to the masked-diffusion NELBO and providing a principled motivation for training-free test-time adaptation; the proofs in Appendix B are reasonably complete and the reduction to the standard NELBO when y is absent is a useful sanity check.

The two algorithmic components (quantized expectation with a straight-through estimator through the LFQ codebook, and posterior-confidence-based anchored remasking) are clearly motivated, and the ablation study (Figure 6, §C.3) disentangles their contributions, showing that quantized expectation fixes sampling bias and anchored remasking prevents discarding informative tokens.

Empirically strong: APS outperforms prior discrete samplers (G2D2, SGDD) across linear and nonlinear inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet, and is often competitive with strong continuous baselines while being substantially faster (15 steps, ~55s vs. PSLD ~720s at 512). The same-prior comparison in Table 7 (APS vs. G2D2 under identical compute and backbone) is a particularly fair and convincing control.
Broad applicability demonstrated: training-free reference-based stylization on MMaDA and reward-guided steering of a 7B diffusion LLM (Dream) show the method extends beyond standard inverse problems.

Thorough supporting material: complexity analysis (§C.5, showing O(KL) vs. the exponential exact marginalization), noise-robustness sweeps (Table 9), hyperparameter ablations (Table 5, 6), and an honest limitations section covering tokenizer quality, base-model weakness, and the approximate (non-asymptotically exact) nature of the sampler.
weaknesses: There is a gap between the theory and the implemented objective. The derived bound (Eq. 8) is a tilted cross-entropy/likelihood objective, but the practical loss (Algorithm 1) is an L1 reconstruction loss plus a VGG perceptual loss with a tuned coefficient; the theoretical objective's normalizing constant is dropped and two further approximations (first-order Taylor, straight-through) are layered on. The paper is candid about this ('surrogate optimization objective'), but it means the central claim of a 'principled' sampler is only loosely connected to what actually runs, and the perceptual loss itself contributes to the gains (Table 7 shows G2D2 also improves with the perceptual loss).

Heavy test-time optimization: 100 Adam steps on the full logit table at each of 15 reverse steps, with an aggressive learning rate (1.0), plus a strong CFG scale. This raises questions about sensitivity to optimization hyperparameters, potential mode collapse toward measurement consistency at the expense of prior fidelity (visible as over-smoothing in some results), and limited analysis of when the surrogate diverges from the true posterior.

Evaluation scale is modest: 100 images per dataset/task (Appendix C.8), matching G2D2's protocol but still limiting statistical strength; the qualitative claims are supported but PSNR/LPIPS differences on some tasks (e.g., inpainting, motion deblur in Table 2) are within ranges that 100 samples may not resolve.

The question-answering evaluation is thin: 20 prompts generated by another LLM, judged by reward models from the same model family (Qwen3-0.6B reward, Qwen3-8B oracle), with a single qualitative example. This is weak evidence for the '21.99% improvement' claim and the reward-family overlap creates a circularity risk.

The quantized expectation replaces x^l with the current posterior estimate x_φ(z_t) as if it were ground truth; the accuracy of this substitution (and its interplay with the Taylor approximation) is asserted via locality/smoothness assumptions but not empirically validated, e.g., by measuring the surrogate-vs-true likelihood gap.

Originality is moderate: likelihood tilting of reverse transitions, STE through quantizers, and anchor-prioritized unmasking are each established ideas (ADLM, MaskGIT-style remasking, straight-through quantization); the contribution is a well-engineered and well-evaluated combination tailored to masked discrete diffusion rather than a fundamentally new principle.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely relevant gap: training-free posterior sampling for masked discrete diffusion models with purely discrete token embeddings, where gradient-based guidance is not directly applicable.

The derivation in Appendix B is careful: it provides a pathwise variational upper bound (Theorem B.1) and a test-time variant (Theorem B.2) that cleanly separates the pretrained NELBO, an adaptation-gap log-ratio term active only at masked positions, and a measurement-consistency term.

The evaluation is broad: linear (SR, Gaussian/motion deblur, inpainting) and nonlinear (HDR, nonlinear blur) inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet, plus stylization and question answering with a 7B diffusion LM, with ablations (Fig. 6, Tables 5-7) and a noise-robustness study (Table 9).

The complexity analysis (Appendix C.5) is honest about the exponential cost of exact marginalization (O(K^L)) and motivates the O(KL) plug-in surrogate, and runtime is reported against baselines (Table 8).
Limitations are discussed candidly, including tokenizer quality, approximate (non-asymptotically exact) posterior sampling, style-extractor dependence, and failure cases (Fig. 15).
weaknesses: A substantial gap exists between theory and algorithm. The test-time bound (Theorem 3.3) is subsequently abandoned in practice: the actual objective (Eq. 8) replaces the tilted per-token terms with a heuristic surrogate 'L * -log q(y|x̂)' derived via a first-order Taylor argument plus a plug-in straight-through approximation, adds an L1 + VGG perceptual reconstruction loss not present in the bound, and drops the normalizing factor. The theorems therefore provide mostly motivational rather than actual support for the method, weakening the 'theoretical results' claim.

The core mechanism is essentially test-time optimization of the full logit table with Adam (M=100 inner steps per reverse step, 15 steps, i.e., 1500 gradient iterations per image), which is a heavy and familiar recipe rather than a principled sampler; the paper itself concedes the method sacrifices asymptotic correctness and introduces bias relative to exact MCMC. Novelty over G2D2 and ADLM (Rout et al., 2025a), whose anchoring idea the remasking explicitly follows in training-free form, appears incremental.

Key quantitative evaluations rest on very small sets: only 100 FFHQ and 100 ImageNet images, and the QA benchmark comprises just 20 prompts judged by reward models from the same model family (Qwen3-0.6B reward, Qwen3-8B judge), raising concerns about statistical reliability and reward-model bias. The 21.99% 'gain' headline is based on this tiny setup.

The comparison protocol disadvantages continuous baselines: benchmark images are upsampled to the discrete model's native resolution before corruption and downsampled for evaluation, which changes the effective degradation and plausibly inflates APS/APS-L PSNR/LPIIPS relative to methods evaluated at native resolution; a same-prior ablation (Table 7) shows much smaller margins than the headline tables.

The 'quantized expectation' reduces to an expectation over codebook embeddings propagated via the straight-through estimator — a well-known trick — and the anchoring/remasking uses per-token confidence under the posterior estimate; neither is analyzed for failure modes such as error accumulation from prematurely committed anchor tokens, beyond qualitative ablation on a single example.

No explicit code release is promised; reproducibility relies on the public MMAxDA codebase plus appendix hyperparameters, and given the sensitivity suggested by the hyperparameter sweeps (Table 5) and 100-step inner optimization, independent reproduction may be fragile.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: training-free posterior sampling for masked discrete diffusion with purely discrete token embeddings, where existing approaches (G2D2's Gumbel relaxations, SGDD's split Gibbs sampler) struggle due to sparse gradients or exponential complexity in sequence length.

Solid theoretical grounding: Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 derive variational upper bounds that reduce to the standard masked-diffusion NELBO when measurements are absent, and the appendix proofs (pp. 14–23) carefully handle boundary conditions, per-step KL terms, and the two-case (masked/unmasked) analysis. The bound clarifies why lightweight test-time adaptation suffices instead of retraining.

The two technical components are well-motivated and cleanly separated: quantized expectation converts an intractable O(K^L) measurement marginalization into a tractable O(KL) surrogate via expected codebook embeddings with a straight-through estimator (complexity analysis in §C.5.1 is explicit and convincing), while anchored remaking is a principled training-free analogue of ADLM's anchor-token idea that uses posterior rather than prior confidence.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 4 linear and 2 nonlinear inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet, stylization, and question answering with a 7B diffusion LLM. APS consistently beats discrete baselines (G2D2, SGDD) and is often competitive with strong continuous methods (DiffPIR, PSLD) at substantially lower runtime (Table 8: 15 steps, ~6x faster than PSLD at 512x512).

Thorough ablations (§C.3, Figure 6) that isolate standard remasking vs. quantized expectation vs. anchored remasking, hyperparameter sweeps (perceptual coefficient, optimization steps), noise robustness (Table 9), a same-prior same-compute comparison against G2D2 (Table 7) showing gains arise from the algorithm rather than the prior, and a 1000-image extension (Table 11).

Honest limitations section (tokenizer quality, weaker base model vs. Flux/SD3.5, stylization backbone dependence, approximation bias relative to exact MCMC), plus failure cases, licenses, and a reproducibility statement with full pseudocode and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Gap between theory and practice: the practical objective (Eq. 8) departs substantially from the derived bound—quantized expectation relies on a first-order Taylor approximation and a local smoothness assumption for A∘D that is not verified, and the normalizing factor log Z is dropped. The bounds are thus motivation rather than guarantees for the actual sampler, and no quantification of this approximation error is provided.
Evaluation scale is modest: headline results use only 100 images per benchmark (following G2D2's protocol), which limits statistical confidence; only SR is extended to 1000 images.

The QA experiment (§4.4) is weak: 20 hand-curated prompts generated by Qwen2.5-3B, judged by LLM reward models (Qwen3-0.6B for optimization, Qwen3-8B as 'oracle'), with potential judge/reward circularity; the claimed 21.99% gain rests on this small and self-constructed benchmark.

Anchored remasking is closely related to ADLM (Rout et al., 2025a); the novelty claim is confined to a training-free variant, and the paper could better delineate the contribution relative to that work.

Test-time optimization cost is nontrivial: 100 inner Adam steps per reverse step (15 steps) through the decoder; while Table 8 shows acceptable runtimes, sensitivity to this inner loop and possible pathological cases are not fully characterized.

Some quantitative comparisons against continuous baselines involve different underlying priors and resolution-upsampling protocols (following G2D2), so cross-paradigm comparisons should be interpreted cautiously; the paper is generally careful here but headline phrases like 'up to 35.82% improvements' highlight best cases.
